title: Highweb & Page Group Inc. (June 2015 TCC) SR&ED Case
subject: TCC informal-procedure appeal testing documentation standards for web and software SR&ED claims.
summary: Highweb & Page Group Inc. v. The Queen (2015 TCC 137) is a Tax Court of Canada SR&ED decision affecting Canadian corporations claiming software development credits. Justice Bocock dismissed the appeal for 2007 and 2008, leaving only STA2 – Phase II allowed, and held that SR&ED claims require detailed, contemporaneous records of hypotheses, tests, and results kept as work progresses.
metaDescription: Review the June 2015 Tax Court of Canada decision for Highweb & Page Group Inc. regarding Canadian SR&ED tax credit eligibility.

body.text: Executive Summary and Case Background

On June 8, 2015, Justice Randall S. Bocock of the Tax Court of Canada, signing at Edmonton, Alberta, following a hearing in Toronto, Ontario, on April 1 and 2, 2015, issued the reasons for judgment in Highweb & Page Group Inc. v. The Queen, 2015 TCC 137 (Docket: 2014-1703(IT)I). Heard under the Court's Informal Procedure, the appeal concerned the disallowance by the Minister of National Revenue (the "Minister"), following review by the Canada Revenue Agency ("CRA"), of Scientific Research and Experimental Development ("SR&ED") expenditures claimed by the Appellant—$25,200 for the 2007 taxation year (Phase I) and $37,975 for the 2008 taxation year (Phase II)—while the Minister allowed SR&ED Investment Tax Credits ("ITCs") of $2,704 for the 2008 taxation year in respect of a single claimed advancement ("STA2 – Phase II"). Despite being adjudicated under the Informal Procedure—which technically precludes the decision from serving as binding formal precedent under section 18.28 of the Tax Court of Canada Act—Justice Bocock's trenchant judicial analysis regarding the evidentiary threshold for contemporaneous documentation and the distinction between commercial outcomes and experimental processes has been repeatedly adopted in subsequent Tax Court of Canada jurisprudence, elevating Highweb & Page Group to a foundational authority in Canadian SR&ED litigation.
The Taxpayer's Claim and Technical Architecture

The Appellant, Highweb & Page Group Inc. ("Highweb"), carries on the business of marketing and designing digital software and web-based accessibility systems, which help small- and medium-sized businesses manage internal server and web-based applications, content, and business processes through its proprietary "iFactum" software suite ("iFactum"), a program already being sold before the SR&ED work was undertaken. For the 2007 and 2008 taxation years, Highweb claimed SR&ED expenditures and related ITCs for work, carried out by its president, Mr. Sarmiento, together with one assistant, aimed at "universalizing" iFactum's compatibility with other commercial operating system platform programs (Phase I, 2007) and with commercial web-based server platforms (Phase II, 2008)—in short, updating and modifying iFactum to work with updated or new third-party system server and web-based software. Highweb structured its technical submissions around discrete Scientific or Technological Advancements ("STAs"), comprising six claimed advancements in Phase I (STA1 to STA6 – Phase I) and four in Phase II (STA1 to STA4 – Phase II); the second Phase II advancement, designated STA2 – Phase II, was the only one the Minister accepted.

In argument, Highweb's agent submitted, relying on CRA Information Circular 86-4R3, that "system uncertainty" existed even where, at first glance, technological uncertainty might not. In the discipline of software engineering, system uncertainty is alleged to arise when a claimant integrates multiple technologies or software components—each of which may be individually understood—into a complex unified architecture where interlocking constraints and unpredictable interactions prevent competent professionals from predicting whether or how the integrated system will function. Highweb contended that its systematic investigation yielded six technological advancements in Phase I and four in Phase II—including the STA1 – Phase I claim that rendering iFactum interoperable with the full spectrum of commercial software and hardware platforms was a breakthrough in system flexibility—and that this work satisfied the statutory definition of experimental development.
The Tax Authority's Challenge

Upon technical review by a CRA Research and Technology Advisor ("RTA"), Mr. Pelissero, who prepared a 16-page SR&ED Technical Review Report, the Minister issued a highly selective partial allowance that framed the precise legal boundaries of the dispute: the amounts, dates, and other criteria were not disputed, so the single issue was whether the work beyond STA2 – Phase II constituted SR&ED. The Minister disallowed all six Phase I advancements and STA1, STA3, and STA4 of Phase II, the RTA finding that the contemporaneous documentation (weekly work journals and trouble tickets) showed industry programming techniques that a trained IT professional would perform under similar circumstances, that no new scientific or technological knowledge was generated, and—for several of the claims—that the claimed advancement was better understood as a "statement of business fact" describing what had to be done.

The Minister did, however, allow a single, narrowly defined claimed advancement—STA2 – Phase II—for which it allowed ITCs of $2,704 in the 2008 taxation year; that work ran from February 18 to April 6, 2008, and the RTA accepted 246 hours by Mr. Sarmiento (supervision, experimentation, programming) and 153 hours by a second person (tester/programmer) as eligible. That accepted advancement involved a specific inter-platform conflict: an incompatibility, not readily resolvable with existing, accessible products, between the data-type mapping of QueryBeans and .NET and Java, which required research to devise code allowing such data to be shared between .NET and Java. The CRA accepted that STA2 – Phase II was supported by records—a Request Ticket History and a Time Tracking log—containing details of the work done, and the Court later noted that the individual testing and modification of functions in phased protocols had been duly recorded. Conversely, the CRA disallowed the nine other claimed advancements, concluding that they consisted of correct techniques that a trained IT professional would apply—such as using Java technology and J# as intended, relying on publicly available porting documentation, identifying the host operating system by well-known methods, and retrofitting code to comply with web-service and SOA specifications—rather than a systematic investigation generating new knowledge.
Governing Statutory and Jurisprudential Framework

The eligibility of R&D tax incentives in Canada is governed by the federal Income Tax Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.) (the "Act"). Subsection 248(1) of the Act defines "scientific research and experimental development" as a "systematic investigation or search that is carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis". For commercial software and industrial claimants, eligibility almost invariably rests on paragraph (c) of the definition—"experimental development"—which requires work undertaken for the purpose of achieving technological advancement for the purpose of creating new, or improving existing, materials, devices, products, or processes, including incremental improvements thereto. Crucially, subsection 248(1) carves out explicit statutory exclusions in paragraphs (e) through (k), disqualifying work with respect to market research or sales promotion under paragraph (e), as well as quality control or routine testing of materials, devices, products, or processes under paragraph (f). Where activities satisfy subsection 248(1), qualifying expenditures—which, as the Court noted, must be made on SR&ED related to the taxpayer's business, carried on in Canada and directly undertaken by the taxpayer pursuant to subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i)—are pooled and deducted under section 37 of the Act (including paragraph 37(8)(b)), while corresponding ITCs are calculated and claimed under subsections 127(5) and 127(9).

To operationalize the statutory language of subsection 248(1), Canadian tax courts apply the five criteria outlined by Justice Bowman, as an aid in assessing whether work constitutes SR&ED, in Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Ltd. v. The Queen, [1998] 3 CTC 2520, 1998 CanLII 553 (TCC) (the citation used by the Court in Highweb), and endorsed by the Federal Court of Appeal in RIS-Christie Ltd. v. Canada, [1998] F.C.J. No. 1890 (FCA). Drawing upon the CRA's administrative guidelines—historically Information Circular 86-4R3, later consolidated into the 2012 and 2015 Eligibility of Work for SR&ED Investment Tax Credits Policy (the "CRA Eligibility Policy") and the 2021 Guidelines on the Eligibility of Work for SR&ED Tax Incentives, which the Tax Court in 6379249 Canada Inc. v. The Queen, 2015 TCC 77, confirmed as a reliable interpretive guide—the court evaluates five sequential questions, all of which must be answered in the affirmative on a balance of probabilities.

Under this cumulative judicial test, the court first examines whether there was a technical risk or technological uncertainty that could not be removed by routine engineering or standard procedures. Second, the inquiry determines whether the person claiming to be doing SR&ED formulated hypotheses specifically aimed at reducing or eliminating that technological uncertainty. Third, the court assesses whether the procedure adopted accorded with established and objective principles of the scientific method, including the formulation, testing, and modification of hypotheses. Fourth, the analysis verifies whether the process resulted in a technological advance, meaning an advancement in the general understanding of technology. Fifth and finally, the court requires proof that a detailed record of the hypotheses, tests, and results was kept as the work progressed.
The Court's Final Holding

Justice Bocock dismissed Highweb's appeal for both the 2007 and 2008 taxation years on the basis that the Appellant did not undertake SR&ED beyond that already recognized by the Minister (STA2 – Phase II) and, because the Appellant elected the Informal Procedure, made no order as to costs. The Court acknowledged that some incremental technological uncertainty and advancement may well have occurred within other components of Phase I or Phase II, but concluded that the Appellant failed to show, more likely than not, that the disallowed work involved a systematic investigation aimed at a genuine technological knowledge gap, failed to identify the precise hypotheses, experiments, and knowledge gained, and showed manifest disregard of the scientific method's fundamental requirement for detailed and current recordkeeping as the work progressed.
Core Legal and Evidentiary Failures

A forensic examination of the ruling in Highweb & Page Group reveals four interconnected legal, technical, and evidentiary failures that dismantled the taxpayer's appeal. Each deficiency highlights a recurring structural vulnerability in Canadian corporate SR&ED claims and illustrates how deficiencies in one element of the Northwest Hydraulic framework inevitably cascade to invalidate subsequent criteria.
Conflation of Commercial Objectives with Technological Uncertainty ("Statements of Business Fact")

The primary substantive defect in Highweb's presentation of STA1 – Phase I was its inability to distinguish between commercial product attributes and underlying technological uncertainty. In its technical claim descriptions, Highweb relied heavily on promotional, result-oriented hyperbole, asserting most notably: "This breakthrough in system flexibility created unlimited scalability."

In the Technical Review Report summarized in Appendix 1 of the decision, the CRA characterized several of Highweb's claimed advancements (STA4 and STA5 – Phase I and STA1, STA3, and STA4 – Phase II) as "better understood as a statement of business fact and what had to be done," and at paragraph 18 Justice Bocock held that technological uncertainty requires a genuine gap in knowledge—not knowledge that exists but is merely unknown to the claimant, nor a gap soluble by applying other products through the usual techniques of skilled software developers. When a taxpayer asserts that its software architecture achieved "unlimited scalability," "seamless cross-platform compatibility," or "enhanced system flexibility," the taxpayer is merely articulating a functional business objective or a commercial performance characteristic. As the Tax Court previously established in Zeuter Development Corporation Inc. v. The Queen, 2006 TCC 597 (at paragraphs 22 and 24), resolving functional uncertainties associated with a commercial project or creating a new, complex product does not automatically equate to resolving a technological uncertainty or achieving a technological advance.

Under the first criterion of Northwest Hydraulic and section 2.1.1 of the CRA Eligibility Policy, scientific or technological uncertainty exists only where whether a given objective can be achieved, or how to achieve it, cannot be known or determined on the basis of generally available scientific or technological knowledge or experience. Crucially, the jurisprudence emphasizes that a claimant must do far more than declare that the path to achieving a project objective was unknown to its internal coding team; the claimant must identify specifically what is lacking in the scientific or technological knowledge base that created the obstacle. The Court found that, because readily available programs such as J# and JavaScript formed the bedrock of the work, the uncertainty was not a technological knowledge gap but one of selective trial and procedural sequencing—knowing which available products, applied in the correct sequence with routine modifications, would best enhance the existing but outdated iFactum software—so Highweb failed at the threshold question of eligibility.
Misapplication of the "System Uncertainty" Doctrine and Failure to Segregate Routine Engineering

To rescue its claim from being classified as standard software development, Highweb leaned heavily on the doctrine of "system uncertainty". In Canadian SR&ED practice, system uncertainty occurs when individual components or subsystems are well-known, deterministic, and commercially available, yet their integration into a unified system introduces interlocking constraints, conflicting parameter requirements, or unpredictable behaviour whose resolution is not reasonably predictable by a competent professional in the field. While Canadian courts recognize system uncertainty as a valid category of technological uncertainty—as demonstrated in Gabie v. The Queen (1998), Dave's Diesel Inc. v. The Queen, 2022 TCC 61, and Buhler Versatile Inc. v. The King, 2023 TCC 15—the mere size, scale, or architectural complexity of a software system cannot support an inference that system uncertainty existed.

Justice Bocock's comparison of the allowed STA2 – Phase II undertaking with the nine disallowed claimed advancements, together with his finding that the agent's system-uncertainty submission was factually not apparent from the evidence, provides an authoritative blueprint on how system uncertainty interacts with "routine engineering". Under Northwest Hydraulic (at paragraph 16), routine engineering encompasses techniques, procedures, and data that are generally accessible to competent professionals in the field.

In the allowed sub-claim (STA2 – Phase II), Highweb isolated a narrow, objective architectural impasse: "There existed an incompatibility, not readily resolvable with existing, accessible products, between data type mapping of QueryBeans and .NET and Java, which required research to devise code to allow sharing of such data between .NET and Java." This discrete segment satisfied the statutory mandate because, as the Court found, considerably more recorded information was generated for it; the identified uncertainties in the differential encoding of .NET and Java platforms were resolved through individual testing and modification, duly recorded, in phased protocols; a technique was devised to reconcile shared data types between .NET and JavaScript-based platforms; and knowledge was gained not by proving the hypothesis but by learning from an outcome proved by a negative result.

However, Highweb committed a classic legal overreach by claiming nine further advancements—six in Phase I and three in Phase II—beyond the single one the Minister recognized. For these other claims, the Court found no comparably defined, examined, analyzed, or resolved technological experiment or advancement, and no sufficient concurrent records showing that the system and internet incompatibilities were analyzed sufficiently to establish a need for technological experimentation. On the evidence, the enhancement of iFactum consisted of applying existing, newly released third-party products and debugging code deficiencies and incompatibilities between iFactum and other platforms using usual software design techniques—usual and customary product updating that is prolific in the industry. Justice Bocock characterized this as product research and development—Highweb's core business of software design and modification of its existing product, applied to commercially enhance iFactum's marketability (citing C.W. Agencies Inc. v. Canada, 2002 DTC 6740)—rather than scientific research or experimental development.
Absence of a Structured Process of Experimentation and Hypothesis-Driven Investigation

Even if a claimant successfully establishes a baseline technological or system uncertainty, subsection 248(1) mandates that the uncertainty be addressed through a "systematic investigation or search... by means of experiment or analysis". As articulated in the CRA Eligibility Policy and endorsed by the Tax Court, tax advisors and claimants must rigorously distinguish between a "systematic approach to carrying out work" and the "systematic investigation or search" required by the statute.

A professional software engineering firm almost always employs a systematic approach to carrying out work by utilizing structured development methodologies, tracking feature tickets, conducting code reviews, and executing automated regression testing. Yet, disciplined software project management does not constitute the scientific method under the second and third criteria of Northwest Hydraulic. A statutory systematic investigation requires formulating one or more explicit, testable hypotheses specifically designed to reduce or eliminate the identified technological uncertainty, planning and executing controlled experiments or technical analyses to test those hypotheses, and developing logical, causal conclusions based on the empirical results of each test to modify the hypothesis before initiating subsequent iterations.

Highweb failed to prove that its developers engaged in hypothesis-driven experimentation in any claimed advancement other than STA2 – Phase II; its two overriding hypotheses were assembled by its agent only at the conclusion of one-and-a-half days of evidence, after precise questioning from the Bench, and it was not clear that they had been documented when the work was undertaken. Where developers encounter coding errors or integration bugs and resolve them by iteratively modifying code parameters until the software compiles and functions—without conducting a formal root-cause analysis to understand why a specific technological requirement was not met before testing the next hypothesis—the jurisprudence classifies the activity as routine debugging or "trial and error". As reinforced in Hypercube Inc. v. The Queen, 2015 TCC 65, Flavor Net Inc. v. The Queen, 2017 TCC 179, and Canafric Inc. v. The King, 2023 TCC 108, unguided trial and error or standard web programming does not satisfy the scientific method and cannot generate a technological advancement under the fourth criterion of Northwest Hydraulic.
Failure to Retain Contemporaneous Documentation of the "Thought Process" and Expenditure Allocation

The most decisive blow to Highweb's appeal—and the exact legal point for which Highweb & Page Group is repeatedly cited in modern Canadian tax litigation—was its failure to meet the fifth criterion of Northwest Hydraulic: maintaining a detailed, contemporaneous record of hypotheses, tests, and results as the work progressed.

At trial, Highweb's documentary evidence consisted of time tracking sheets and approximately 37 trouble-ticket entries for Phase I and 17 for Phase II (computer-based "post-its" describing challenges and next steps in very general terms), while Mr. Sarmiento described the uncertainty, advancement, and work almost exclusively by reference to the CRA's Technical Review Report rather than to any organized technical records created by Highweb. In rejecting this outcome-centric approach, Justice Bocock delivered two seminal pronouncements at paragraphs 20 and 22 of the judgment. First, at paragraph 20, Justice Bocock held, citing Northwest Hydraulic (at paragraph 16), that a "detailed record of the hypotheses … be kept as the work progresses," and at paragraph 22 he found that the CRA Technical Review Report—which recorded Mr. Sarmiento's interview commentary given after the work—was not a suitable substitute for contemporaneous record keeping. Second, Justice Bocock declared at paragraph 22: "While evidence of the outcome is important, it is critical to technological advancement that the rigours of adherence to the scientific and experimental method be kept on a detailed and concurrent basis with the conduct of the experiments."

This judicial standard—subsequently adopted verbatim in Mac & Mac Hydrodemolition Services Inc. v. The Queen, 2017 TCC 256 (at paragraph 10), and Concept Danat Inc. v. The Queen, 2019 TCC 32 (at paragraph 24)—establishes that proving what was built is legally insufficient; the documentary record must prove how and why each experimental step was taken in real time. Unlike the allowed STA2 – Phase II sub-claim, for which the Request Ticket History and Time Tracking log contained details of the work and the phased testing was duly recorded, the disallowed claims were supported only by scant concurrent records—general trouble tickets and time sheets—with nothing approaching the detailed step-by-step logging, analysis, and measurement needed to show the iterative rejection and modification of hypotheses. As later underscored in National R&D Inc. v. The Queen, 2020 TCC 47 (at paragraph 71), experiment tables or technical summaries reconstructed after the fact for a CRA audit carry zero evidentiary weight and severely damage witness credibility.

Although the amounts, dates, and other expenditure criteria were expressly not in dispute in Highweb, documentation deficits of this kind can also undermine expenditure verification under section 37 of the Act. When a project contains both an eligible experimental core (such as the STA2 – Phase II investigation) and stretches of ineligible routine application (such as the other claimed advancements), the taxpayer bears the burden of providing accurate, contemporaneous records of hours worked by each employee on specific SR&ED tasks, rather than relying on global percentages or retroactive estimates, a principle strictly enforced in Hypercube Inc., 2015 TCC 65 (at paragraph 48), and Concept Danat Inc., 2019 TCC 32 (at paragraphs 25 and 54).
Comparative Summary Table

The following table maps each statutory and jurisprudential requirement examined in Highweb & Page Group Inc. v. The Queen against the taxpayer's specific legal or evidentiary failures and the governing standard of proof enforced by the Tax Court of Canada.

headers: Highweb's Specific Evidentiary or Legal Failure
The Tax Court's Standard of Proof & Analytical Benchmark

cells: 1. Scientific or Technological Uncertainty
Income Tax Act, s. 248(1); Northwest Hydraulic, 1998 CanLII 553 (TCC) (Criterion 1); CRA Eligibility Policy, s. 2.1.1

Relied on inflated commercial hyperbole in STA1 – Phase I ("This breakthrough in system flexibility created unlimited scalability"), language the Court found reflected no genuine knowledge gap, much as the CRA labelled several other claims a mere "statement of business fact". Failed to define what was lacking in the publicly accessible technological knowledge base.

The claimant must prove on a balance of probabilities that an objective shortcoming or field knowledge-gap in the current state of technology prevented the capability from being achieved through standard procedures or routine engineering.
2. System Uncertainty vs. Routine Engineering
Income Tax Act, s. 248(1)(c) & (f); Northwest Hydraulic (para. 16); Zeuter Development, 2006 TCC 597

Claimed broad "system uncertainty" across the entire iFactum updating project. Beyond STA2 – Phase II (the QueryBeans .NET/Java data-type incompatibility the Minister allowed), claimed nine further advancements that the Court found to be usual product updating, application of existing products, and debugging.

System uncertainty requires proving unpredictable, non-linear interactions among known components that existing products cannot resolve. Applying existing products and debugging incompatibilities with usual software design techniques is product research and development, not SR&ED (Highweb, paras. 18 and 21).
3. Formulation of Specific Hypotheses
Northwest Hydraulic (Criterion 2); RIS-Christie Ltd. v. Canada, [1998] F.C.J. No. 1890 (FCA)

Confused functional product goals (achieving platform compatibility and scalability) with testable scientific hypotheses. Only in STA2 – Phase II did the record show hallmarks of technological uncertainty ("incompatibility," "not resolvable with existing products," "required research") leading to a developed hypothesis; the two overriding hypotheses were assembled only at the hearing.

The claimant must formulate explicit, causal hypotheses prior to testing that specify the technological variables being manipulated and are specifically aimed at reducing or eliminating the defined technological uncertainty.
4. Systematic Investigation & Scientific Method
Income Tax Act, s. 248(1); Northwest Hydraulic (Criterion 3); Flavor Net, 2017 TCC 179; Canafric, 2023 TCC 108

Conflated a systematic approach to software development (standard coding and project management) with a statutory systematic investigation. Failed to show iterative hypothesis modification based on causal failure analysis.

The procedure must accord with objective principles of the scientific method: formulating hypotheses, executing phased testing, and conducting rigorous analysis to understand why a requirement was not met before initiating the next test iteration.
5. Technological Advancement
Income Tax Act, s. 248(1)(c); Northwest Hydraulic (Criterion 4); Zeuter Development (para. 24)

Equated enhancing the existing iFactum product for compatibility with newly released third-party platforms with a technological advance. Could not articulate any new knowledge generated that advanced the general understanding of software technology in any claim other than STA2 – Phase II.

Creating a new or complex commercial product is not per se a technological advance. The process must generate new technological knowledge (including the rejection of a hitherto untested hypothesis) that advances the general understanding of competent professionals in the field.
6. Contemporaneous Record of the "Thought Process"
Northwest Hydraulic (Criterion 5); Highweb & Page Group, 2015 TCC 137 (paras. 20 & 22); Mac & Mac, 2017 TCC 256; Concept Danat, 2019 TCC 32

Relied almost exclusively on the CRA's after-the-fact Technical Review Report rather than contemporaneous experimental records for all claims other than STA2 – Phase II. Failed to retain dated documentation demonstrating the engineering "thought process" as the work progressed.

"While evidence of the outcome is important, it is critical to technological advancement that the rigours of adherence to the scientific and experimental [method]" be kept on a detailed and concurrent basis with the conduct of the experiments (para. 22), through detailed step-by-step logging that captures the contemporaneous thought process.
7. Expenditure Segregation & Time Tracking
Income Tax Act, ss. 37 & 127; Hypercube Inc., 2015 TCC 65 (para. 48); Concept Danat, 2019 TCC 32 (para. 25)

Not at issue in Highweb, where the amounts, dates, and other criteria were undisputed; the eligible STA2 – Phase II hours (246 and 153 hours) were accepted because the time tracking log and request ticket history detailed the work done.

Claimants must maintain accurate, contemporaneous records of hours worked tied directly to specific SR&ED tasks. Post-hoc percentage estimates or unsegregated project-wide labour pools are rejected by the Court.

body.text: Two Applied Remedial Case Studies

To translate the legal holdings of Highweb & Page Group Inc. v. The Queen into actionable compliance protocols for Canadian corporate taxpayers, the following two industry case studies examine realistic technical projects that suffer from the exact legal, contractual, and evidentiary defects identified by Justice Bocock. Each case study demonstrates step-by-step how the taxpayer can restructure its project governance, technical documentation, contract terms, and experimentation tracking to overcome the Court's objections and fully satisfy the statutory SR&ED requirements under the Act.
Case Study 1: Enterprise FinTech SaaS — Cross-Runtime Serialization and Distributed Concurrency Architecture
Initial Project Posture and Legal Pitfalls

Aethelgard Cloud Solutions Inc. ("Aethelgard"), a Canadian-controlled private corporation ("CCPC") based in Calgary, Alberta, develops an enterprise SaaS treasury management platform. In its current taxation year, Aethelgard undertakes a $1.8 million software engineering project to integrate its legacy Java Virtual Machine ("JVM") monolithic transaction engine with a new, high-frequency algorithmic risk engine written in Rust and compiled to WebAssembly ("Wasm").

In its unreviewed draft Form T661, Aethelgard claims 100% of the salaries of 12 software developers over the entire 12-month release cycle, alongside $400,000 paid to an arm's-length Canadian software consultancy. The draft claim exhibits four fatal Highweb defects. First, mirroring the STA1 pitfall, Box 242 and Box 246 of Form T661 rely on promotional hyperbole, stating: "Our breakthrough zero-latency hybrid cloud architecture achieved unlimited horizontal scalability and seamless real-time cross-platform compatibility." Second, mirroring Highweb's claim of nine advancements beyond the single STA2 – Phase II advancement the Minister allowed, only six weeks of the project involved investigating a genuine memory-safety and garbage-collection deadlock across the JVM-to-Wasm Foreign Function Interface ("FFI"), whereas the remaining 46 weeks consisted of building REST APIs, user dashboards, and propagating the FFI wrapper across 80 standard business microservices. Third, in violation of paragraphs 20 and 22 of Highweb, the engineering team deleted failed Git branches upon merging the final working code into production, leaving only the finished commercial repository and high-level Jira feature tickets. Fourth, the Master Services Agreement ("MSA") with the Canadian consultancy is structured as a generic staff-augmentation and feature-delivery contract with no reference to subsection 248(1) or section 37 of the Act.
Step 1: Restructuring Project Governance and Scope Segregation

To prevent the CRA from disallowing most of the claim during audit—and to establish unmatched institutional credibility—Aethelgard's Chief Technology Officer and tax counsel must decouple the commercial product roadmap ("Project Horizon") from the statutory SR&ED project ("SR&ED Project 2026-01: Asynchronous Zero-Copy FFI Memory Management under Concurrent JVM Garbage Collection"). Project governance is restructured by instituting a formal "SR&ED Eligibility Gate" at the start of every two-week Agile sprint. Under this governance protocol, work enters the SR&ED pool only when the Lead Architect documents a preliminary literature and benchmark analysis proving that publicly accessible solutions—specifically standard Java Native Interface ("JNI"), Apache Arrow, and GraalVM Truffle polyglot bindings—are incapable of preventing thread lock contention when passing 100,000+ mutable state structs per second between the JVM heap and Wasm linear memory.

Equally critical is enforcing a rigorous administrative cut-off point once the core technological uncertainty is resolved. The moment the custom lock-free ring-buffer FFI protocol is validated in a standalone benchmark environment—which corresponds to the narrowly defined investigation the Minister allowed in Highweb's STA2 – Phase II—governance rules mandate that the SR&ED project code is locked. The subsequent rollout and propagation of that validated protocol across Aethelgard's 80 commercial microservices is automatically routed to commercial cost centres and explicitly segregated from Form T661 as routine software engineering and quality control testing under paragraph 248(1)(f) of the Act.
Step 2: Rewriting Technical Documentation to Eliminate "Statements of Business Fact"

Tax counsel must excise all commercial and promotional adjectives—such as "breakthrough," "unlimited scalability," and "seamless"—from the technical record so the claim cannot be dismissed as a "statement of business fact" (as the CRA characterized several claims in Appendix 1) or as lacking a knowledge gap under paragraph 18 of Highweb. The Form T661 narrative and internal architectural briefs are rewritten to mirror the linguistic hallmarks Justice Bocock identified in STA2 – Phase II (paragraph 20), anchoring the narrative in an objective field knowledge-gap.

Specifically, the revised technological uncertainty narrative states that an architectural memory-model incompatibility, not readily resolvable with existing, accessible FFI bindings or serialization frameworks (specifically JNI, Project Panama, and standard Wasmtime bindings), arose when attempting concurrent zero-copy state sharing between a non-deterministic JVM Garbage Collector ("G1GC") and deterministic Rust/Wasm linear memory. The documentation explains that existing accessible products required either defensive memory copying—which exceeded the 1.5-millisecond latency ceiling by 420%—or pinned heap pointers that induced fatal G1GC stop-the-world compaction deadlocks under concurrent load, creating system uncertainty as to whether a lock-free, epoch-based memory reclamation algorithm could be devised to synchronize JVM safepoints with Wasm linear memory bounds without corrupting heap pointers. Similarly, rather than claiming a business outcome, the technological advancement is articulated as an objective contribution to computer science knowledge: the systematic investigation generated new technological knowledge regarding the interaction between JVM safepoint polling intervals and cross-boundary epoch-based reclamation in WebAssembly runtimes, proving that asymmetric hazard-pointer fencing eliminates G1GC compaction deadlocks at sub-millisecond latencies.
Step 3: Restructuring Contract Terms and Subcontractor Governance

Under subsections 37(1) and 127(9) of the Act, payments to arm's-length Canadian subcontractors qualify for SR&ED treatment only where the contract is for SR&ED (here, experimental development within paragraph (c) of the definition in subsection 248(1)) "directly undertaken on behalf of the taxpayer" within subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i.01), and only 80% of such an expenditure counts as a qualified expenditure for ITC purposes under the definition of "qualified expenditure" in subsection 127(9). Aethelgard executes a formal Amending Agreement and Statement of Work ("SOW") with its Canadian consultancy built around four legal covenants. First, the SOW explicitly mandates experimental development, specifying that the subcontractor is retained not to deliver a commercial software module, but to execute experimental hypotheses and performance analyses under Aethelgard's technical direction to resolve the JVM/Wasm FFI memory incompatibility. Second, payment terms are structured strictly on an hourly time-and-materials basis without commercial "acceptance testing" or "refund-on-failure" warranties, legally proving that Aethelgard bears 100% of the financial and technical risk if the technological hypotheses fail. Third, the contract provides for ab initio intellectual property vesting, stipulating that all source code, failed experimental branches, test telemetry, and resulting technological advancements vest immediately and exclusively in Aethelgard upon creation. Fourth, a granular invoicing covenant obligates the subcontractor to submit weekly invoices itemizing hours by individual developer, cross-referenced to Aethelgard's internal SR&ED Experiment IDs and Git commit hashes, explicitly excluding any routine user-interface or commercial integration tasks.
Step 4: Experimentation Tracking to Capture the Contemporaneous "Thought Process"

To satisfy Justice Bocock's requirement at paragraphs 20 and 22 of Highweb—and to insulate the claim against the post-hoc reconstruction penalties imposed in National R&D, 2020 TCC 47 (at paragraph 71)—Aethelgard implements an automated, immutable "Evidence Ledger" integrated directly into its Git and continuous integration ("CI/CD") pipeline. Repository governance is configured to prohibit deleting or squashing experimental branches, ensuring that every failed iteration (such as exp/SRED-01-jni-direct-bytebuffer, exp/SRED-02-panama-arena-pinning, and exp/SRED-03-hazard-pointer-epoch) is permanently archived with immutable cryptographic commit hashes and timestamps.

Furthermore, developers cannot close an experimental branch without completing a mandatory Hypothesis-Test-Analysis-Conclusion ("HTAC") Markdown template embedded directly in the repository pull-request workflow. For each phased test (Phase I through Phase IV), this contemporaneous artifact records the exact mathematical and architectural hypothesis formulated prior to coding, specifies the experimental test harness parameters, and links directly to dated Prometheus and Grafana flame graphs and JVM crash dumps showing exact empirical failure metrics. Crucially, before the next branch can be opened, the lead engineer must complete the causal analysis section—satisfying both Highweb (paragraphs 20 and 22) and Canafric, 2023 TCC 108—by documenting why the hypothesis failed based on computer science principles and explaining how that specific deduction dictated the modification of the hypothesis in the subsequent test iteration.
Case Study 2: Industrial Automation and Mechatronics — Subterranean Electro-Hydraulic Control System Integration
Initial Project Posture and Legal Pitfalls

Vortex Mechatronics Ltd. ("Vortex"), an industrial equipment manufacturer based in Sudbury, Ontario, designs an autonomous hydro-demolition and rock-scaling robotic boom for deep-shaft mining. The system integrates three known, commercially available subsystems: a high-pressure 40,000-PSI water-jetting hydraulic manifold, a solid-state 3D LiDAR optical perception array, and a deterministic Real-Time Operating System ("RTOS") kinematic controller.

When Vortex combined these subsystems in shop-floor trials, the extreme acoustic shockwaves and dense mist generated by the 40,000-PSI hydro-jetting nozzle caused severe multipathing distortion in the LiDAR point cloud and induced high-frequency harmonic resonance in the hydraulic proportional valves, destabilizing the robotic arm. Vortex spent 10 months overcoming this integration failure and claimed $950,000 in SR&ED expenditures. The claim faces four acute legal pitfalls under Highweb and related Tax Court jurisprudence. First, the CRA RTA contends that Vortex did not face genuine system uncertainty, arguing that the engineers merely adjusted existing PID controller gain settings and LiDAR filtering thresholds within the OEM equipment's normal operating ranges—mirroring the exact fatal defect in Concept Danat Inc. v. The Queen, 2019 TCC 32 (at paragraph 54). Second, like the unsuccessful claimant in Mac & Mac Hydrodemolition Services Inc. v. The Queen, 2017 TCC 256 (which directly applied Justice Bocock's ruling in Highweb at paragraph 22), Vortex relied on "evidence of the outcome" by presenting photographs and video of the final working mining robot alongside initial and final CAD blueprints, but kept no structured records of intermediate failed tests. Third, Vortex built the prototype unit under a $2.2 million commercial purchase order from a major Canadian mining corporation paid in three milestone installments, prompting the CRA to assert that the entire project is funded by a "contract payment" under subsection 127(9) of the Act, reducing Vortex's qualified expenditures under subsection 127(18). Fourth, Vortex's President estimated at year-end that four mechanical engineers and three firmware developers spent "roughly 40% of their time" on SR&ED, identical to the arbitrary estimation methodology rejected in Concept Danat (at paragraph 25) and Hypercube (at paragraph 48).
Step 1: Restructuring Project Governance to Establish True "System Uncertainty"

To elevate the project from routine equipment calibration (Concept Danat) to eligible system uncertainty (Dave's Diesel, 2022 TCC 61; Buhler Versatile, 2023 TCC 15; Highweb STA2 – Phase II), Vortex's Vice President of Engineering establishes a formal System Integration and Experimental Review Board ("SIERB") prior to initiating physical shop-floor modifications. The SIERB compiles an initial "Baseline State-of-Technology Dossier" archiving the OEM technical manuals for the hydraulic valves, LiDAR sensors, and RTOS controller. This dossier objectively proves that operating the optical and kinematic control loop within a 40,000-PSI atomized water-mist and 140-dB acoustic shock environment falls entirely outside the manufacturers' normal operating ranges and existing engineering standards, directly neutralizing the Concept Danat objection.

Furthermore, governance documentation defines the exact interlocking system constraint that created the system uncertainty: when all constituent subsystems are combined to function in unison, reducing the hydraulic valve response time to compensate for nozzle recoil increases fluid pressure transients (water hammer), which in turn amplifies structural vibration at the exact resonant frequency (185 Hz) that blinds the LiDAR micro-electromechanical ("MEMS") mirror stabilization loop. By proving mathematically that existing design methods are inapplicable and that the resolution of these interlocking mechanical, fluid-dynamic, and algorithmic constraints cannot be predicted by a competent professional prior to experimentation, Vortex anchors its project squarely within the legal doctrine of system uncertainty.
Step 2: Implementing Scientific Method Documentation Over Shop-Floor "Trial and Error"

To overcome Justice Bocock's admonition in Highweb (at paragraph 22) and Justice Graham's ruling in Mac & Mac Hydrodemolition (at paragraph 10) that "evidence of the outcome" cannot substitute for documenting "the rigours of adherence to the scientific and experimental [method]," Vortex replaces ad-hoc shop-floor tinkering with a formal Design of Experiments ("DoE") Protocol. Before any physical modification or test is executed on the hydro-demolition rig, the engineering team must author and timestamp a formal Experimental Test Plan ("ETP"). For instance, ETP-04 explicitly states the governing hypothesis: "If an active piezo-electric damping mount is coupled with a Kalman filter modified with a non-Gaussian acoustic-phase-rejection matrix in the RTOS interrupt service routine, harmonic cross-talk between the 40,000-PSI lance recoil and the LiDAR time-of-flight photon counter will be attenuated below the 3-millimeter spatial drift threshold."

During each physical test run, automated data-acquisition ("DAQ") telemetry records raw accelerometer vibration spectra, hydraulic pressure spikes, and LiDAR point-cloud dropout rates into timestamped, immutable log files. When ETP-04 fails due to phase-lag instability at 32,000 PSI, governance rules strictly prohibit the engineers from simply adjusting valve settings by trial and error. Instead, the team must author a dated Post-Test Analytical Memorandum incorporating Bode plots and Fast Fourier Transform ("FFT") spectral analysis to explain why the Kalman filter's covariance matrix diverged under non-linear fluid cavitation. This analytical bridge captures the contemporaneous thought process demanded by Justice Bocock at paragraphs 20 and 22 of Highweb, demonstrating how the rejection of one tested hypothesis logically dictated the formulation of ETP-05.
Step 3: Restructuring Commercial Contracts to Neutralize the "Contract Payment" Exclusion

Under subsection 127(9) of the Act, a disqualifying "contract payment" includes an amount paid or payable to a taxpayer by a taxable supplier, such as a Canadian customer, for SR&ED performed for an arm's-length payer entitled to deduct the work as its own SR&ED expenditure under subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i.01) or (i.1). If the mining client's $2.2 million payment is legally characterized as a contract payment for R&D services, Vortex's qualified SR&ED expenditures are reduced dollar-for-dollar under subsection 127(18). To preserve 100% of its ITC entitlement, Vortex's tax counsel restructures the commercial agreement with the mining client using three clear statutory demarcations.

First, the contract is drafted strictly as a Fixed-Price Commercial Equipment Supply Agreement for the sale of a finished physical chattel—a rock-scaling machine meeting specified functional performance metrics (scaling 45 square metres per hour at less than 5 millimetres overbreak)—containing zero contractual covenants or obligations for Vortex to perform SR&ED on behalf of the purchaser. Second, the Intellectual Property clause explicitly stipulates that the mining customer acquires title solely to the physical machine delivered, whereas Vortex retains 100% exclusive ownership of all underlying engineering designs, RTOS source code, control algorithms, patents, and technological know-how generated during the project. Third, milestone payments are tied strictly to commercial delivery events (Factory Acceptance Testing and Site Commissioning), and the customer holds a standard commercial right to reject the unit and demand a full refund if functional specifications are not met. Because Vortex performs the underlying experimental development entirely on its own behalf to resolve the system uncertainty required to manufacture the commercial good—bearing unconditional financial risk of technological failure and retaining all intellectual property—the customer's payments constitute ordinary commercial revenue rather than disqualifying "contract payments" under subsection 127(9) of the Act.
Step 4: Contemporaneous Labour Costing and Activity-Level Time Tracking

To eliminate the fatal evidentiary defect of retroactive salary estimations (Concept Danat, 2019 TCC 32 at paragraph 25; Hypercube, 2015 TCC 65 at paragraph 48) and prevent the CRA from disallowing most of the project hours as routine fabrication (Highweb, 2015 TCC 137), Vortex deploys a mandatory daily digital time-tracking protocol within its Enterprise Resource Planning ("ERP") system. The ERP ledger is bifurcated into strict commercial and experimental project billing codes. Routine engineering activities—such as CAD drafting of standard structural steel frames, commercial component procurement, standard hydraulic plumbing assembly, and commercial Factory Acceptance Testing—are logged under commercial code VTX-COMM-100 and excluded entirely from the SR&ED claim.

Conversely, experimental codes VTX-SRED-ETP01 through VTX-SRED-ETP12 are restricted exclusively to engineering hours spent formulating hypotheses, writing experimental RTOS filtering algorithms, configuring DAQ instrumentation for DoE trials, executing experimental test runs, and authoring Post-Test Analytical Memoranda. Every daily time entry logged to a VTX-SRED-ETP code requires the engineer to input a mandatory text description citing the exact ETP document number, DAQ telemetry log file, or firmware Git commit hash worked on that day. The Vice President of Engineering audits and digitally signs the timesheet ledger on a bi-weekly basis, establishing an unassailable, contemporaneous audit trail that links every claimed dollar of salary under section 37 directly to the documented experimental thought process required by the Tax Court of Canada in Highweb & Page Group Inc. v. The Queen.
Synthesis of Remedial Governance Across Both Case Studies

The following table synthesizes the remedial mechanisms implemented across both case studies to demonstrate how each intervention directly resolves the legal and evidentiary failures identified in Highweb & Page Group Inc. v. The Queen.

body.text: Strategic Conclusions for Canadian SR&ED Practitioners

The Tax Court of Canada's decision in Highweb & Page Group Inc. v. The Queen, 2015 TCC 137, stands as a watershed moment in Canadian SR&ED jurisprudence. While the statutory text of subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act and the five-part framework of Northwest Hydraulic have remained stable for decades, Justice Bocock's ruling crystallized the modern evidentiary standard required to survive judicial scrutiny. First, tax advisors and corporate claimants must purge commercial marketing language and "statements of business fact" from Form T661 narratives, framing every claim instead around a precise, objective limitation in the publicly accessible scientific or technological knowledge base. Second, where "system uncertainty" is invoked in software or industrial integration projects, claimants must surgically sever the experimental kernel (such as the narrowly defined investigation the Minister allowed in STA2 – Phase II) from the routine engineering effort expended to propagate that solution across the commercial product. Finally, because evidence of a successful commercial outcome cannot prove adherence to the scientific method, Canadian taxpayers must institutionalize real-time, artifact-backed documentation protocols that preserve failed iterations and contemporaneously record the engineering "thought process" as the work unfolds.

outcome: Appeal dismissed; court found insufficient evidence of technological uncertainty, hypothesis testing, and systematic investigation.
